name: Data analysis and evaluation of scientific evidence

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of processing raw experimental data into tables and graphs?
a: To make it easier to identify trends, patterns, and relationships between variables
To increase the physical size of the laboratory report
To hide incorrect or messy numbers from teachers
To turn quantitative values into random guesses

questions.q: What does a line of best fit on a scatter graph represent?
a: A random drawing connecting every single data dot
The overall trend or relationship between variables while smoothing out minor experimental errors
The maximum possible limit of the laboratory equipment
Anomalous results that should be ignored

questions.q: What is an anomalous result in a scientific dataset?
a: The exact mathematical average of all trials
The most accurate measurement recorded in the session
A result that does not fit with the pattern or trend of the rest of the data
The independent variable value chosen for the first test

questions.q: How should an anomalous result typically be handled when calculating a mean value?
a: Include it directly without checking
Multiply it by ten to increase its weight
Ignore the data completely without recording it
Investigate for potential errors, repeat the measurement if possible, and exclude it from the mean calculation

questions.q: What indicates a positive correlation on a line graph showing enzyme activity versus temperature?
a: As temperature increases up to a point, enzyme activity increases
As temperature increases, enzyme activity decreases
The graph line remains completely horizontal with zero slope
All data points form a vertical line

questions.q: What does a negative correlation on an experimental graph signify?
a: The experiment failed and must be restarted
As one variable increases, the other variable decreases
The data numbers are all negative values
No measurements were recorded during the test

questions.q: Why is calculating a mean (average) from repeat readings important for scientific evidence?
a: It makes the data table look longer
It changes the hypothesis automatically
It reduces the effect of random errors and improves data reliability
It increases room temperature

questions.q: When analyzing a bar chart comparing the energy content of different food groups, what do the equal widths of the bars ensure?
a: That the paper is colorful
That the experiment took longer to complete
That the student wrote neatly
Fair visual comparison without misleading the reader

questions.q: What is the correct way to calculate the mean of a set of valid repeat readings (e.g., 12, 14, 13)?
a: Add all the values together and divide by the number of readings
Multiply all the values together
Take only the highest value
Subtract the lowest value from the highest value

questions.q: What does a scatter graph with points scattered randomly across the grid with no visible pattern indicate?
a: The experiment was performed with absolute perfection
There is no apparent relationship or correlation between the variables
The dependent variable is too large to measure
The equipment is digital

questions.q: Why must axis labels on a scientific graph always include both the variable name and its physical unit?
a: To make the graph look decorative
To confuse anyone reading the lab report
To ensure the graph can be interpreted accurately and scientifically
To change the conclusion of the study

questions.q: What is a conclusion drawn from scientific evidence?
a: A list of equipment used before starting
A guess about what you will eat for lunch
A fictional story about science history
A summary statement explaining what the results show, supported directly by processed data

questions.q: What is the difference between data and evidence?
a: Data are the raw measurements collected, whereas evidence is processed data used to support or refute a scientific claim
Data and evidence mean the exact same thing with no differences
Evidence is collected before an experiment, while data is written afterward
Data is qualitative only, while evidence is always digital

questions.q: Why might a scientist repeat an investigation published by another researcher?
a: To copy their homework
To check reproducibility and verify whether the evidence is reliable and valid
To prove that all science experiments fail
To waste laboratory resources

questions.q: What is a limitation in experimental evidence?
a: A rule about wearing safety goggles
The time of day the lesson starts
A factor or restriction (such as equipment resolution) that constrains how far the conclusions can be generalized
The cost of a notebook

questions.q: When evaluating a scientific claim made in an advertisement, what should a student check first?
a: How expensive the product is
Whether the company has a nice logo
Whether the advertisement uses bright colors
Whether the claim is supported by controlled, repeatable experimental evidence

questions.q: What does a steep gradient on a line graph of plant growth over time indicate?
a: A rapid rate of growth over that time period
A very slow rate of growth
That the plant stopped growing entirely
That the measuring ruler was broken

questions.q: Why is it important to examine the scale on graph axes when analyzing published data?
a: To see how much paper was wasted
A non-zero or compressed scale can visually exaggerate or distort trends and relationships
To find out the name of the graph maker
To check the room lighting

questions.q: What is secondary data in scientific enquiry?
a: The second measurement taken in a data table
Your lab partner's personal opinion
Data collected by other researchers, found in books, journals, or databases, used for comparison
Random internet rumors with no source

questions.q: What does evaluating a scientific method involve during data analysis?
a: Leaving the laboratory immediately
Throwing away all data tables
Buying new equipment for the school
Assessing how well the method controlled variables and identifying potential sources of error

questions.q: Why do biological datasets often show more variation between repeat readings than chemistry datasets?
a: Living organisms naturally show biological diversity and individual differences
Living organisms are made of metal
Biology experiments are never repeated
Biology uses no measuring tools

questions.q: What is the purpose of using a line graph rather than a bar chart when plotting continuous data like temperature changes over time?
a: To show percentages in a circle
To show continuous trends and allow estimation of values between measured points
To display disconnected categories
To hide incorrect numbers

questions.q: What does a horizontal line on a distance-time or growth-time graph signify?
a: The variable is increasing rapidly
The variable is decreasing quickly
No change or zero rate of change over that time period
An experimental error occurred

questions.q: When evaluating whether a conclusion is fully supported by evidence, what must a student check?
a: Whether the conclusion matches personal opinions
Whether the font size is large enough
Whether the graphs are drawn in color
Whether every statement in the conclusion is directly backed up by trends seen in the data table or graph

questions.q: What is precision in scientific data collection?
a: How close repeated measurements are to each other
How close a measurement is to the true value
How expensive the measuring equipment is
How fast the data table is filled in

questions.q: What is accuracy in scientific measurements?
a: Getting the same incorrect number ten times
How close a measured result is to the true or accepted value
Writing numbers in neat handwriting
Using the largest beaker available

questions.q: What is the primary risk of drawing a conclusion from a sample size that is too small?
a: The report will take too long to read
The paper will run out of ink
The evidence may not be representative of the wider population, leading to an unreliable conclusion
The room temperature will drop

questions.q: Why might a set of data have high precision but low accuracy?
a: The instruments were read incorrectly or had a systematic calibration error, giving tight clustered wrong results
The students worked too quickly
The data table had too many columns
Random errors were completely eliminated

questions.q: What is a systematic error in experimental data?
a: An error caused by a faulty instrument or flaw in experimental design that shifts all readings consistently in one direction
A random mistake in writing down a number
An accidental spill on the laboratory floor
A sudden change in weather outside

questions.q: What is a random error in measurements, and how can its impact on final evidence be minimized?
a: An intentional change to the independent variable; minimized by stopping the test
An unpredictable variation in readings; minimized by taking repeats and calculating a mean
A permanent flaw in equipment calibration; minimized by buying new desks
A spelling mistake in the conclusion; minimized by using a dictionary

questions.q: When analyzing a pie chart representing energy use in an ecosystem, what do the individual sectors represent?
a: Disconnected random numbers
The exact temperature of each organism
Proportions or percentages of a whole category
Anomalous results

questions.q: Why do scientists peer-review data analyses and conclusions before they are published in scientific journals?
a: To let classmates grade each other's handwriting
To make students rewrite notes ten times
To test typing speed on computers
To check validity, spot errors in data interpretation, and ensure scientific rigor
